L	The Allahabad High Court’s decision in Anamika Tiwari and Others v. State of U.P.
reaffirmed the legal position that a wife is the absolute owner of her streedhan and cannot
ordinarily be prosecuted for criminal breach of trust in relation to property that legally belongs
to her. The dispute arose after matrimonial discord developed between the husband and wife
following their marriage in 2012. The wife had earlier lodged criminal proceedings against her
husband and his family under Sections 498-A and 323 of the Indian Penal Code and provisions
of the Dowry Prohibition Act, alleging harassment and demands for additional dowry.
Subsequently, the husband initiated a counter-complaint alleging that the wife and her
relatives had entered his house and taken away cash, jewellery, and household articles. On
the basis of these allegations, the Magistrate summoned the wife and her relatives for offences
including criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC.
While examining the validity of the summoning order, the High Court analysed Sections 405
and 406 IPC dealing with criminal breach of trust. The Court noted that the offence requires
entrustment of property followed by dishonest misappropriation or conversion of that property
by the person entrusted with it. However, the Court held that streedhan — consisting of gifts
and property given to a woman before, during, or after marriage — remains her exclusive
property. Since the wife herself is the absolute owner of such property, the essential
requirement of “entrustment” by the husband or his family could not exist in relation to her
own ornaments and valuables. Consequently, prosecution under Section 406 IPC against the
wife was legally unsustainable.
The Court further clarified that marriage does not transform streedhan into joint marital
property. Although a husband may, in times of financial distress, temporarily use the wife’s
streedhan, such use does not confer ownership or legal control upon him or his relatives. At
best, the husband carries a moral obligation to restore the property or its equivalent value.
The Court also criticised the Magistrate for issuing the summoning order casually without
properly examining whether the statutory ingredients of criminal breach of trust were
satisfied. Since the allegations against the wife’s relatives were similarly vague and general in
nature, the Court ultimately quashed the entire criminal proceedings.
The judgment reaffirmed broader principles repeatedly recognized by Indian courts, including
in Rashmi Kumar v. Mahesh Kumar Bhada, namely that streedhan remains the sole and
exclusive property of a woman and neither the husband nor the in-laws acquire dominion over
it merely because of marriage. The ruling also highlighted the importance of carefully
scrutinizing criminal complaints in matrimonial disputes to ensure that criminal law is not
invoked mechanically without satisfying essential legal ingredients.

Il.	The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 retains the distinction between kidnapping and
abduction that existed under the earlier criminal law framework. Although both offences
involve taking a person from one place to another, they differ significantly in their essential
ingredients and legal consequences.
Kidnapping is generally regarded as a more specific offence. Under the BNS, kidnapping may
occur in two principal forms: kidnapping from India and kidnapping from lawful guardianship.
These forms of kidnapping are covered under Section 137 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023, while abduction is dealt with under Section 138. Kidnapping from India takes place
when a person is conveyed beyond the territorial limits of India without that person's consent
or without the consent of a person legally authorised to provide such consent. Kidnapping from
lawful guardianship occurs when a minor or a person of unsound mind is taken or enticed
away from the keeping of their lawful guardian without the guardian's consent. In the case of
kidnapping from lawful guardianship, the consent of the minor is legally irrelevant. What
matters is whether the lawful guardian consented to the removal of the minor.
Abduction, on the other hand, is defined more broadly. A person commits abduction when, by
force or deceitful means, he or she compels or induces another person to move from one place
to another. Unlike kidnapping, abduction can be committed against a person of any age.
Further, abduction is not an independent offence in every situation. It generally becomes

Another important distinction lies in the means employed. Kidnapping from lawful
guardianship may occur even without force or fraud. Merely enticing a minor away from a
lawful guardian may be sufficient. In contrast, abduction necessarily requires the use of force
or deceitful means. Therefore, a person who persuades a seventeen-year-old to voluntarily
leave home may be guilty of kidnapping from lawful guardianship even if no force is used.

Courts have repeatedly emphasised that the object of provisions relating to kidnapping is to
protect minors and persons incapable of making informed decisions. The law seeks to preserve
the authority of lawful guardians and prevent exploitation of vulnerable individuals.
Abduction provisions, meanwhile, focus on the wrongful methods used to move a person from
one place to another and the criminal purpose behind such movement.
Thus, while kidnapping and abduction may appear similar, the age of the victim, the role of
consent, the presence of force or deceit, and the underlying purpose are crucial factors that
determine which offence has been committed under the BNS.

Il.	The law of torts imposes liability on persons whose activities cause harm to others, even in the
absence of criminal intent. One of the most important principles governing hazardous
activities is the doctrine of strict liability. This doctrine originated in the English case of
Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), where the court held that a person who, for his own purposes,
brings onto his land and keeps there anything likely to cause mischief if it escapes, must keep
it at his peril. If the thing escapes and causes damage, the person is liable for the
consequences.
The rule of strict liability applies only when there is a non-natural use of land and when a
dangerous thing escapes from the defendant's control. However, the doctrine is subject to
several exceptions. A defendant may avoid liability if the escape was caused by an act of God,
the act of a stranger, the plaintiff's own fault, statutory authority, or where the plaintiff
consented to the risk.
India initially adopted the doctrine of strict liability. However, industrial development and the
rise of hazardous industries exposed the limitations of the rule. Following the Oleum Gas Leak
incident in Delhi, the Supreme Court recognized that enterprises engaged in inherently
dangerous or hazardous activities possess greater resources and profit from such activities.
Consequently, they must bear a higher degree of responsibility.
In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court evolved the doctrine of absolute
liability. According to this principle, an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently
dangerous activity is absolutely liable to compensate all those affected by any accident
resulting from such activity. Unlike strict liability, no exceptions are available under absolute
liability. The enterprise cannot escape responsibility by arguing that the harm was caused by
an act of God, sabotage by a stranger, or any other traditional defence.
Another important distinction is that strict liability applies generally to dangerous things that
escape from a person's land, whereas absolute liability specifically targets enterprises carrying
out hazardous or inherently dangerous activities. Moreover, under absolute liability,
compensation is often linked to the enterprise's capacity and resources so that the deterrent
effect remains meaningful. Thus, while both doctrines impose liability without proof of
negligence, absolute liability imposes a far more stringent and socially responsive standard
than strict liability.
Source: Adapted from principles discussed in the Law of Torts, the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher
(1868), and the Supreme Court judgment in Oleum Gas Leak Case.

IV.	The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 was enacted by Parliament
to curb paper leaks, impersonation, and organised cheating in public examinations. It received
the President's assent and was later brought into force on 21 June 2024, vide notification S.O.
2422(E). Although the Act was enacted before the NEET-UG 2024 controversy, it was brought
into force amid heightened public concern over paper leaks and examination malpractice,
including controversies such as NEET-UG 2024, which had shaken public confidence in the
integrity of competitive examinations.
The Act applies to examinations conducted by public examination authorities listed in its
Schedule, covering bodies such as the UPSC, SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards, banking
recruitment agencies, and the National Testing Agency. It defines "unfair means" broadly to
include the leakage of a question paper or answer key, colluding with others to effect such
leakage, and unauthorised access to or possession of a question paper or an Optical Mark
Recognition sheet, along with related acts done for monetary or wrongful gain.
On punishment, the Act distinguishes between individuals, service providers, and organised
crime. A person resorting to unfair means or committing offences under the Act may be
punished with imprisonment of not less than three years, extendable to five years, and a fine
up to ten lakh rupees. The penalties become far heavier for organised crime. Where a person
or group of persons, including an examination authority, service provider, or any other
institution, commits an organised crime, the punishment is imprisonment of not less than five
years, extendable to ten years, with a fine of not less than one crore rupees. If an institution is
involved in such an organised crime, its property is subject to attachment and forfeiture, anda
proportionate cost of the examination is recovered from it. The Act also declares offences under
it to be cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.
A key protective feature is that a candidate is not liable for action under the Act and continues
to be governed by the existing administrative provisions of the concerned public examination

V.	Contempt of court is a legal mechanism designed to protect the authority, dignity and effective
functioning of courts. In India, the power to punish for contempt is derived not only from the
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 but also from Articles 129 and 215 of the Constitution, which
declare the Supreme Court and High Courts to be courts of record with the power to punish for
contempt. Broadly, contempt may be civil or criminal. Civil contempt refers to the wilful
disobedience of a court's judgment, order or undertaking. Criminal contempt includes acts that
scandalise or lower the authority of a court, prejudice judicial proceedings or obstruct the
administration of justice.
However, the law also recognises that courts are public institutions and are not immune from
fair criticism. The Contempt of Courts Act provides that fair and reasonable criticism of
judicial acts made in good faith does not amount to contempt. The distinction lies in whether
the criticism merely questions a judicial decision through reasoned analysis or whether it
seeks to undermine public confidence in the administration of justice through baseless or
malicious allegations.

This distinction became the subject of national debate following the Supreme Court's suo motu
proceedings concerning an NCERT Class VIII Social Science textbook. The textbook contained
a chapter discussing issues such as judicial corruption, delays in the justice delivery system
and the shortage of judges. The Supreme Court observed that portions of the chapter prima
facie appeared to lower the authority of the judiciary and ordered a complete withdrawal of
the textbook from physical and digital circulation while issuing notices regarding possible
contempt proceedings against responsible officials. The Court also directed the removal of
certain contributors from future publicly funded curriculum projects. The Union Government
and NCERT subsequently tendered an unconditional apology and recalled the textbook. The
subsequent developments also indicated that directions affecting future engagement of
contributors were revisited, thereby keeping the focus of the controversy on the balance
between contempt jurisdiction, institutional accountability and academic freedom.
The controversy generated significant public discussion on the balance between judicial
accountability and the law of contempt. While supporters of the Court's action argued that
educational material should not contain statements capable of eroding public confidence in the
judiciary without adequate foundation, critics questioned whether academic discussion of
institutional shortcomings could amount to contempt, particularly where supported by
publicly available information. Legal scholars noted that contempt jurisdiction should
ordinarily be exercised with caution, as excessive use may have implications for academic
freedom and freedom of speech guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a), subject to the reasonable
restriction relating to contempt of court under Article 19(2). Thus, the episode highlighted the
continuing constitutional challenge of balancing institutional integrity with democratic
criticism.
